properties.vocals: Ellington rarely centered himself as a vocalist; his bands regularly featured dedicated singers (e.g., Ivie Anderson, Al Hibbler) while his arrangements emphasized instrumental voices, call-and-response patterns and ensemble harmonies rather than solo singing by Ellington.
properties.biography: Born Edward Kennedy Ellington in Washington, D.C., in 1899, he acquired the nickname "Duke" as a youth and studied piano and music while attending local schools. He began performing professionally as a teenager and formed early ensembles that eventually became the Duke Ellington Orchestra. Moving to New York in the early 1920s, Ellington secured high-profile engagements (notably at Harlem's Cotton Club) and built a reputation for distinctive arrangements, unusual voicings and long-form compositions. Over a career spanning the 1910s to his death in 1974, Ellington composed across styles, collaborated closely with Billy Strayhorn, nurtured many sidemen who became stars in their own right, and produced a vast catalog that bridged popular, dance, and concert music.
properties.known_for: Composing hundreds of jazz standards, leading the Duke Ellington Orchestra for decades, pioneering orchestral jazz arrangements and elevating jazz as a concert genre.
properties.description: Edward Kennedy 'Duke' Ellington (1899–1974) was a towering American composer, pianist and bandleader who led the Duke Ellington Orchestra for more than five decades, composing thousands of works and countless jazz standards. He helped elevate jazz to concert-hall respectability through sophisticated orchestration, extended-form compositions and a unique focus on tone color and individual soloists within a large ensemble. Ellington's career included landmark residencies (notably the Cotton Club), prolific studio recordings for major labels, close collaboration with arranger-composer Billy Strayhorn, and enduring songs such as "Mood Indigo," "Sophisticated Lady," and "In a Sentimental Mood."
notable_songs: It Don't Mean a Thing (If It Ain't Got That Swing)
properties.cultural_impact: Ellington reshaped the cultural standing of jazz, demonstrating that it could be a sophisticated, compositional art form suitable for concert halls and international tours. He expanded the palette of big band arranging, promoted individual voices within an orchestra, influenced generations of composers and performers, and became an emblematic figure of 20th-century American music and African-American achievement. His works remain central to jazz education and repertoire, and posthumous honors (including a special Pulitzer Prize citation) attest to his lasting influence.
properties.performance_style: Ellington led with a discreet, authoritative presence, emphasizing tight ensemble playing, carefully crafted voicings and featuring soloists; his performances balanced polished, often understated bandleading with occasional theatrical touches and a focus on tonal color rather than showmanship.

properties.biography: Born in 1909 in Chicago, Illinois, Benny Goodman began playing clarinet at a young age and quickly rose through the ranks of jazz musicians. By the early 1930s, he had formed his own band and gained national attention with his energetic swing style. Goodman's 1938 Carnegie Hall concert is considered a landmark event in jazz history. Throughout his career, he was known for his technical mastery, leadership, and efforts to integrate his bands racially. He continued performing until his death in 1986.
properties.known_for: Virtuosic clarinet playing, pioneering swing music, and breaking racial barriers in jazz.
properties.description: Benny Goodman was a pioneering American jazz clarinetist and bandleader who played a central role in popularizing swing music in the 1930s and 1940s. Known as the 'King of Swing', Goodman led one of the most popular big bands of the swing era and was instrumental in breaking racial barriers in music by integrating his band. He was also a skilled classical clarinetist, performing and recording classical repertoire.
properties.cultural_impact: Benny Goodman was a key figure in the swing era and helped bring jazz into mainstream American culture. His integrated bands challenged racial segregation in music, and his performances helped elevate jazz as a respected art form.
properties.performance_style: Goodman's performance style was dynamic and engaging, combining technical virtuosity with charismatic stage presence, often leading large swing orchestras with precision and flair.

properties.biography: Born in 1904 in Iowa, Glenn Miller began his musical career as a trombonist and arranger. He played with various bands before forming his own orchestra in 1938, which quickly rose to fame with a unique sound and popular recordings. Miller's band became a symbol of the swing era, and he also contributed to the war effort by leading the Army Air Force Band. His mysterious disappearance in 1944 during a flight over the English Channel remains a notable event in music history.
properties.known_for: Distinctive big band sound with clarinet-led reed section, popular swing hits, and contributions to wartime morale through music.
properties.description: Glenn Miller was an American trombonist, arranger, composer, and bandleader in the swing era. He led one of the best-selling big bands of the late 1930s and early 1940s, known for hits like 'In the Mood' and 'Moonlight Serenade.' His music was characterized by a distinctive clarinet-led reed section sound. Miller's career was cut short when he disappeared in 1944 during World War II while traveling to entertain U.S. troops overseas.

properties.biography: Born Miles Dewey Davis III in Alton, Illinois, in 1926, Davis moved with his family to East St. Louis and grew up in a middle-class household where music was encouraged. properties.description: Auntie Mame (1958), directed by Morton DaCosta and starring Rosalind Russell, Forrest Tucker and Coral Browne, is a comedy-drama adapted from the popular stage and literary source. It follows a young orphan placed with his flamboyant aunt in 1928 Manhattan, whose bohemian lifestyle clashes with a conservative estate executor as they endure social snobbery and the Depression. Equal parts madcap comedy and sentimental drama, the film focuses on mentorship, nonconformity, and the ways unconventional love shapes coming-of-age identity. Rosalind Russell's tour-de-force performance anchors a colorful ensemble through both comic set pieces and heartfelt moments.
properties.plot_summary: After his father's sudden death, a young boy is placed in the care of his free-spirited aunt in 1928 Manhattan, and is swept into her bohemian, party-filled world. Her unconventional lifestyle soon brings her into conflict with the executor of the estate, who objects to her influence and seeks more conservative guardianship for the boy. As the years pass and the Depression brings hardship, their bond is tested by custody battles, social snobbery, and romantic upheavals, but the aunt remains determined to broaden his life and protect him. The story balances broad comedy and theatrical set pieces with heartfelt moments about family, mentorship, and resilience in changing times.

properties.description: A Poem Is a Naked Person is a Les Blank-directed music documentary originating from the early 1970s that documents recording and life at Leon Russell's Oklahoma compound during 1972–1974. Featuring Leon Russell along with visiting musicians such as George Jones and Willie Nelson, the film assembles concert footage, studio sessions and local vignettes into a free-form, observational portrait. Long withheld from wide release, the piece is often described as a lyrical, intimate celebration of musical creativity and Southern everyday life rather than a conventional biography. Its tone is warm, dreamlike and music-forward, highlighting collaboration and the process of making music.
properties.plot_summary: Over a three-year period in the early 1970s, a filmmaker lived on and around a musician's Oklahoma compound to record studio sessions, concerts, and everyday life. The film assembles vignette-like moments—rehearsals, performances, local color, and intimate informal scenes—rather than a traditional biographical narrative. Guest performers and session players drift through the footage, and the camera often lingers on small gestures and landscapes that frame the music. The result is a free-form, observational portrait that privileges mood and musical presence over exposition.

properties.description: Carousel (1956), directed by Henry King and adapted from the Rodgers and Hammerstein stage musical (itself derived from Ferenc Molnár's Liliom), stars Gordon MacRae, Shirley Jones and Cameron Mitchell in a dramatic fantasy musical. Musically rich and visually widescreen, the film pairs show-stopping numbers with a dark, melancholic narrative and explores themes of fatherhood, guilt and forgiveness. Its emotional tone is solemn and deeply moving, appealing to viewers who appreciate classic, character-driven musical drama.

properties.description: Guess Who's Coming to Dinner (1967), directed by Stanley Kramer and starring Spencer Tracy, Katharine Hepburn, and Sidney Poitier, is a comedy-drama about a liberal San Francisco family whose values are tested when their daughter arrives engaged to a Black physician. The film unfolds largely over one day and a single dinner, using intimate, dialogue-rich scenes to examine racism, family loyalty, and the clash between principle and fear. Noted for its powerful performances and a climactic paternal monologue, the movie balances moments of gentle humor with serious social commentary. Its tone is earnest and emotionally affecting, inviting viewers to reflect on love, acceptance, and social change.
properties.plot_summary: A well-to-do liberal couple in San Francisco confront their own beliefs when their adult daughter returns home engaged to an African American physician. Over the course of a single day and a dinner, polite conversation gives way to heated, heartfelt debates about race, family expectations, and social consequences. The visitors and parents exchange candid confessions and moral reckonings, culminating in a long, emotional speech that forces everyone to reckon with love versus prejudice. The film stays focused on intimate performances and dialogue rather than external action.

properties.biography: Born Dino Paul Crocetti on June 7, 1917 in Steubenville, Ohio, to Italian immigrant parents, Dean Martin left school young and worked a variety of jobs before pursuing entertainment. In the 1940s he began performing as a singer in nightclubs and on radio; his comedic partnership with Jerry Lewis brought nationwide fame and a movie contract. After the duo split in 1956, Martin established himself as a solo recording artist with hits in the 1950s and 1960s, starred in Hollywood films (including collaborations with John Wayne and in Rat Pack ensembles), and became a television star with variety and roast programs. His easygoing persona, trademark slurred delivery and impeccable phrasing made him an enduring figure in American popular culture until his death in 1995.

properties.biography: Born March 17, 1919, in Montgomery, Alabama, Nathaniel Adams Coles moved with his family to Chicago and then to Los Angeles, where he learned piano and started performing as a teenager. In the late 1930s he formed the Nat King Cole Trio (noted for its piano-led, guitar-and-bass rhythm), becoming a major jazz attraction in the 1940s with recordings that blended jazz improvisation and popular songcraft. In the late 1940s and 1950s he shifted toward lush, orchestrated pop recordings and became an international star with hits like "Mona Lisa" and "Unforgettable." Cole also broke new ground as an African-American performer on radio and television, hosting The Nat King Cole Show in 1956–57. He remained an influential figure until his death in 1965 from lung cancer.

properties.description: Nat King Cole (born Nathaniel Adams Coles) was an American jazz pianist and vocalist whose warm, smooth baritone and elegant phrasing made him one of the 20th century's most popular singers. Cole broke racial barriers as one of the first African-American entertainers to host a national television variety program and achieved major crossover success on pop and jazz charts worldwide.

properties.description: Auntie Mame (1958), directed by Morton DaCosta and starring Rosalind Russell, Forrest Tucker and Coral Browne, is a comedy-drama adapted from the popular stage and literary source. It follows a young orphan placed with his flamboyant aunt in 1928 Manhattan, whose bohemian lifestyle clashes with a conservative estate executor as they endure social snobbery and the Depression. Equal parts madcap comedy and sentimental drama, the film focuses on mentorship, nonconformity, and the ways unconventional love shapes coming-of-age identity. Rosalind Russell's tour-de-force performance anchors a colorful ensemble through both comic set pieces and heartfelt moments.
properties.plot_summary: After his father's sudden death, a young boy is placed in the care of his free-spirited aunt in 1928 Manhattan, and is swept into her bohemian, party-filled world. Her unconventional lifestyle soon brings her into conflict with the executor of the estate, who objects to her influence and seeks more conservative guardianship for the boy. As the years pass and the Depression brings hardship, their bond is tested by custody battles, social snobbery, and romantic upheavals, but the aunt remains determined to broaden his life and protect him. The story balances broad comedy and theatrical set pieces with heartfelt moments about family, mentorship, and resilience in changing times.

Musically rich and visually widescreen, the film pairs show-stopping numbers with a dark, melancholic narrative and explores themes of fatherhood, guilt and forgiveness. properties.plot_summary: Fifteen years after his death a carnival barker in the afterlife is granted one day on Earth to try to make amends to his widow and their daughter. The story blends musical spectacle with a melancholy, moral core and a spiritual view of second chances.

Episodes often place the family at the center of larger community events—church, school, harvests, disputes with local merchants and neighbors, and responses to natural disasters or epidemics—showing how neighbors cooperate and conflict as they confront hardship, loss and occasional joy. Over the series the children grow from youngsters into adults, relationships evolve (including marriages and departures), and episodes alternate between domestic scenes, moral dilemmas and moments of open, pastoral life on the prairie.

properties.biography: Born Pierino Ronald Como in 1912 in Canonsburg, Pennsylvania, Perry Como began his career as a barber before moving into music. He gained early experience singing with big bands and orchestras in the 1930s and 1940s. Como's breakthrough came with RCA Victor in the mid-1940s, where his recordings of songs like 'Till the End of Time' and 'Catch a Falling Star' became major hits. He transitioned successfully into television in the 1950s, becoming a beloved figure with his calm demeanor and smooth vocal delivery. Como continued to record and perform into the 1980s, leaving a lasting legacy in American popular music.

properties.biography: Born Dino Paul Crocetti on June 7, 1917 in Steubenville, Ohio, to Italian immigrant parents, Dean Martin left school young and worked a variety of jobs before pursuing entertainment. In the 1940s he began performing as a singer in nightclubs and on radio; his comedic partnership with Jerry Lewis brought nationwide fame and a movie contract. After the duo split in 1956, Martin established himself as a solo recording artist with hits in the 1950s and 1960s, starred in Hollywood films (including collaborations with John Wayne and in Rat Pack ensembles), and became a television star with variety and roast programs. His easygoing persona, trademark slurred delivery and impeccable phrasing made him an enduring figure in American popular culture until his death in 1995.

Rising from working-class beginnings in Steubenville, Ohio, Martin found success as part of a comedy duo with Jerry Lewis in the late 1940s and early 1950s, then as a solo recording artist and film star. He was a core member of the Las Vegas Rat Pack alongside Frank Sinatra and Sammy Davis Jr., hosted The Dean Martin Show and The Dean Martin Celebrity Roast on television, and left a lasting catalog of standards and hits that bridged pop, jazz and lounge traditions.
